Here is my provocation. Choosing a prompt is a creative act, so an AI image can be art. Who wants to push back?
I will. If a prompt is a brushstroke, is a restaurant order a recipe?
Nice. But photographers also press a button, and nobody says a photograph is not art anymore.
That comparison is not unreasonable. A photographer still chooses where to stand, when to wait and what to leave out.
And a person using a generative program chooses among hundreds of images. Is that not a kind of choosing?
It is. The problem is the dataset. Those images were learned from artists who never agreed to it.
So your objection is not really about art. It is about authorship and consent.
Maybe that is the more honest question. Not is it art, but whose work is inside it.
Half this table walked in thinking this was a simple yes or no. Hardly anyone thinks so now.
I am still ambivalent. But I am ambivalent about better questions.

I have covered auctions for years, and most of them are, frankly, not very exciting. People raise paddles, a number goes up, someone says sold. That October evening in London was different. The painting was one of the last lots of the night, and the bidding went well past a million pounds. The auctioneer brought down the hammer, and then, a second or two later, an alarm started sounding from somewhere near the painting. Everyone turned. The canvas began sliding down through the bottom of its frame, and it came out underneath in long, thin strips. People gasped. A few laughed. Staff members rushed over. And then, about halfway through, it simply stopped, so the top of the picture was still there and the bottom hung in ribbons. Within a few days the artist had given the half-shredded work a new title, and when it came back to auction three years later, it sold for many times the original price. As protests against the art market go, it was not a complete success.

People often ask me whether the machine is the real artist in my studio, so let me describe what actually happens. I write code that trains a model on material I have chosen, often my own drawings, and then I ask it to suggest variations. Think of it as a very fast, very strange assistant. It shows me possibilities I would never have imagined, and most of them are terrible. I still decide what to keep, what to change and what to throw away, and that deciding is where I think the work lives. Now, I want to be honest about what worries me. Some of the popular image tools were trained on the work of millions of artists who were never asked and are not credited, and I do not think that problem is going away by itself. As for whether what I make is art, the question is not uninteresting, but I have stopped arguing about it. I would rather ask what the work makes people notice.
